problem: Same conflation: the chart shows 74 islands; about 130 is the number Tupaia named.

fix.digest: Having guided the ship through the Society Islands, Tupaia begins working with the British on a chart of the islands he knows, reciting names, bearings and sailing distances. The finished chart placed 74 of the roughly 130 islands he named, across a radius of about 2,000 miles. It is the only map on the voyage made from Polynesian knowledge rather than European survey.

problem: 'against Cook's standing orders' is not supported: the coxswain fired after warning shots, which Cook's orders allowed in defence of the boats. Characterising it as a breach of orders is an interpretation not in the journals.

fix.digest: On the evening of the landing, four ship's boys left guarding a boat are challenged by local men, and in the confusion Te Maro, a Ngāti Oneone rangatira, is shot dead by the coxswain of the pinnace. The British heard wailing ashore through the night. In 2019 Ngāti Oneone's spokesman described Te Maro's purpose that day as providing food for his people, a chiefly task, and said his actions gave his people a future.

problem: 'I can by no means justify my conduct' does not match Cook's journal. Cook wrote that humane readers 'will cencure my conduct in fireing upon the people in this boat nor do I my self think that the reason I had for seizing upon her will att all justify me'. He conceded that seizing the canoe could not be justified, but defended the firing as self-defence once its crew attacked. The digest inverts this.

fix.quote: will cencure my conduct in fireing upon the people in this boat
fix.digest: Hoping to take people aboard and win their friendship with gifts, Cook's boats try to intercept a canoe; a musket fired over it makes its crew fight, and the boat crews fire into it, killing two to four men. Three young men who leap into the water are taken aboard, clothed and fed. Cook admits that humane readers will censure him and that his reason for trying to seize the canoe cannot justify him, though he argues his men had to fire once attacked.

problem: Matches the inverted reading in entry 10: Cook conceded the seizure could not be justified and defended the firing, not the other way round.

fix.note: Monkhouse fires in the press on the riverbank; Tupaia is the only one who can speak to anyone; Cook concedes the attempt to seize the canoe cannot be justified yet defends the firing; Banks marks the day black. Ngāti Oneone remember Te Maro as a chief doing his duty to feed his people.

problem: 'like a fool' is a modern English rendering of Humboldt's German ('wie die Narren') set in quotation marks as if it were his wording.

fix.digest: Humboldt's first diary volume, the Cumaná book, ends here. He and Bonpland left by sea for La Guaira and Caracas carrying their first crates of plants, and the second volume opens with Caracas. Behind them were the cave of the oil-birds at Caripe, an earthquake and the meteor storm. The man who had arrived running about like a fool among the plants was now running a full programme of measurements.

problem: Lewis has no journal for 25 September 1804, so only four keepers (Clark, Ordway, Gass, Whitehouse) wrote about the standoff, not five.

fix.digest: For the winter the Corps spent at the Mandan villages, Lone Dog's count paints a calumet, the ceremonial pipe, and the keeper's gloss says the people danced the calumet dance before going to war. The count says nothing about the Americans who had faced down the Teton Lakota that autumn. The confrontation that fills pages in four American journals did not become this Dakota keeper's sign for the year. The Teton side of 25 September survives only through the expedition's own pages and later Lakota histories.

It took him until 1809, and a large armed escort after the failed 1807 attempt, to get home.

fix.note: Every American keeper wrote about the standoff, each stressing a different side of it: Clark's anger, Ordway's loaded guns, Gass's boast. The Lakota account of the day is not in these sources.
